title: Welcome to Kodstigen
excerpt: A free, open path from your first line of code to your first developer role, now running entirely in your browser as a static site.
author: Sebastian Larsson
content:
# Welcome to Kodstigen

Kodstigen is a free programming curriculum: interactive lessons, quizzes, and coding challenges across 28 learning paths, from Python and JavaScript to Kubernetes, Solidity, and quantum computing with Qiskit.

## Everything runs in your browser

There is no account to create and no server holding your work. The site is a static build, and every runnable code block executes locally on your machine:

- **Python** runs through [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org), a full CPython build compiled to WebAssembly. `numpy`, `pandas`, and `scikit-learn` load on demand.
- **JavaScript** runs in a Web Worker with a hard timeout, so an accidental infinite loop can't lock up the page.
- **TypeScript** is stripped with [Sucrase](https://sucrase.io) and then run as JavaScript.
- **Lua** runs on [wasmoon](https://github.com/ceifa/wasmoon), and **C** on a WebAssembly build of picoc.
- **HTML** blocks render in a sandboxed iframe you can edit live.

Try it, edit any code block in a lesson and press **Run**:

```python
for n in range(1, 16):
    if n % 15 == 0:
        print("FizzBuzz")
    elif n % 3 == 0:
        print("Fizz")
    elif n % 5 == 0:
        print("Buzz")
    else:
        print(n)
```

## Where to start

- Browse the [courses](/courses) and pick a path, every lesson is open, in any order.
- Warm up on the [coding challenges](/challenges) if you'd rather write code than read about it.
- New to programming entirely? [Programming Basics: Your First Steps](/courses/sample-programming-basics) assumes nothing.

Questions, bug reports, or course ideas are always welcome, the contact link lives in the footer of every page.

title: Three New Courses: Data Mining, Big Data, and GSAP
excerpt: Find patterns in messy data, learn what changes when one machine isn't enough, and animate the web with GSAP. Three courses, 27 lessons.
author: Sebastian Larsson
content:
# Three New Courses: Data Mining, Big Data, and GSAP Three courses landed today, 27 lessons between them. Two extend the Python path in a direction it didn't cover before, and one adds animation to the JavaScript path. ## Data Mining with Python The [machine learning course](/courses/machine-learning-fundamentals-with-scikit-learn) teaches you to train a model. [Data Mining with Python](/courses/data-mining-with-python) is about the messier work around it: what patterns are hiding in data nobody has labeled, and which of them are worth acting on. Nine lessons cover CRISP-DM, exploring and cleaning data with pandas, feature engineering and encoding, association rules, k-means segmentation, TF-IDF text mining, and anomaly detection, then a final project on a deliberately messy retail dataset. Association rules are the lesson to look at first. "Customers who bought X also bought Y" is everywhere, and it hides a trap the course builds from scratch so you can see it: ```python baskets = [ {'bread', 'butter', 'milk'}, {'bread', 'butter'}, {'bread', 'milk'}, {'beer', 'chips'}, {'bread', 'butter', 'jam'}, {'beer', 'chips', 'salsa'}, {'milk', 'cereal'}, {'bread', 'butter', 'milk', 'jam'}, {'beer', 'chips'}, {'bread', 'milk', 'cereal'}, ] n = len(baskets) def support(items): return sum(1 for b in baskets if set(items) <= b) / n def rule(x, y): conf = support(x | y) / support(x) return 'conf=%.2f lift=%.2f' % (conf, conf / support(y)) print('beer -> chips', rule({'beer'}, {'chips'})) print('bread -> milk ', rule({'bread'}, {'milk'})) ``` Run it: `beer -> chips` comes back with confidence 1.00 and a lift of 3.33, `bread -> milk` with confidence 0.67 and a lift of 1.33. Confidence alone makes those look like the same kind of rule in different strengths. Lift is what separates a real pattern from a coincidence dressed up as one, and a rule with 90% confidence and a lift of 1.0 is worth exactly nothing. The whole course runs here in the page, `numpy`, `pandas`, and `scikit-learn` load into the sandbox on demand. ## Big Data Fundamentals [Big Data Fundamentals](/courses/big-data-fundamentals) is deliberately not a "learn Spark" course, though Spark is most of it. It's about what changes when the data no longer fits the tool you were using. It opens with the arithmetic for *not* building a cluster, because half a billion rows sounds like a distributed systems problem and often turns out to be a few gigabytes of Parquet that a laptop handles fine. From there: MapReduce and combiners written in plain Python, columnar storage and partitioning, Spark's driver/executor/partition model, DataFrames and Spark SQL, shuffles and skew, Structured Streaming with event time and watermarks, and lakehouse table formats with pipeline orchestration. The final project is a design document plus a local implementation that has to prove it's idempotent. The shuffle is the thread running through all of it. Once you've watched a combiner reduce ten million records to fifty *before* anything crosses the network, the difference between `reduceByKey` and `groupByKey` stops being trivia: ```python from collections import Counter logs = ['GET /home', 'GET /pricing', 'GET /home', 'POST /login', 'GET /home', 'POST /login', 'GET /pricing', 'GET /home'] partitions = [logs[:4], logs[4:]] partials = [] for part in partitions: local = Counter(line.split()[1] for line in part) partials.append(local) print('this machine sends', len(local), 'records instead of', len(part)) total = Counter() for p in partials: total.update(p) print(dict(total)) ``` The PySpark snippets in the course are for reading, and for running against a real cluster or a local `pyspark` install, so they render as plain code. The MapReduce and pandas blocks run right in the lesson. ## GSAP and ScrollTrigger CSS transitions run out of road quickly. Sequencing, mid-flight control, and scroll-linked playback are where GSAP starts, and ScrollTrigger is what most people come for. [GSAP and ScrollTrigger](/courses/gsap-and-scrolltrigger) covers tweens, eases and stagger, timelines and the position parameter, ScrollTrigger's start/end/toggleActions, scrub and pin, scroll-driven timelines and parallax, then responsiveness with `gsap.matchMedia` and `prefers-reduced-motion`, and four patterns you can lift straight into a project: batched reveals, a horizontal scroll rail, a counter, and a hide-on-scroll header. Every demo is a live preview you can edit. Press **Preview**, then change the numbers: ```html
``` One thing the course insists on: a `prefers-reduced-motion` branch is part of the work, not a nice-to-have. Parallax and large scroll-driven movement genuinely make some people ill, and the OS setting is how they tell you. The `gsap.matchMedia` lesson shows the pattern that handles it without leaving anything stuck at `opacity: 0`. ## Start here - [Data Mining with Python](/courses/data-mining-with-python) - [Big Data Fundamentals](/courses/big-data-fundamentals) - [GSAP and ScrollTrigger](/courses/gsap-and-scrolltrigger) All free, no account, in any order. Every quiz is graded in your browser, and nothing you type leaves your machine.
